newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Foster's to fund buyback from cash, debt.
newsitem.headline: Foster's to fund buyback from cash, debt.

text.p: Foster's Brewing Group Ltd on Thursday said it would fund its A$625 million share buyback from cash flows and existing lines of debt.

Foster's chief executive Ted Kunkel told reporters after announcing the buyback of a 13.0 percent stake held by Asahi Breweries Ltd that the company's net debt-to-equity ratio would jump to 70 percent but he viewed this as comfortable.
"That's a very, very comfortable level for us," he said.
"It reduces the weighted cost of capital significantly. Debt is significantly cheaper than equity these days ..."
Kunkel said he could easily see this gearing level "floating up or floating down" over time.
"It's true our gearing will increase but only to a level which is perfectly acceptable for a company with our healthy cash flow prospects," he said.

In an announcement that had been expected by investors and analysts for a number of months, Foster's said the buyback was part of a two-pronged deal to clear its share registry of two long term investors.
The company would pay A$2.49 per share for the Asahi stake, which represents the bulk of its 270.3 million shares.
Foster's also said 36.5 percent shareholder Broken Hill Pty Co Ltd would place all but 100 million of its 716.6 million Foster's shareholding to institutions and retail investors at A$2.49 per share.

BHP, Australia's largest company and a blue-chip neighbour of Foster's in Melbourne, said it would offer the remaining shares to BHP shareholders. BHP said it would book a profit of about A$75 million on the deal.
BHP stock closed 14 cents down at A$18.83.

Foster's asked the Australian Stock Exchange (ASX) earlier on Thursday afternoon for a trading halt to be placed on its shares pending an announcement which would affect more than 50 percent of its issued capital.
The company said the buyback deal with Asahi was part of an arrangement in which the Japanese brewer and BHP had committed to dispose of all their Foster's shares.

Foster's president and chief executive officer Ted Kunkel said the Asahi buyback price represented a five percent discount to Foster's average price in calendar 1997. Foster's shares were three cents lower at A$2.60 ahead of the trading halt.
"Following completion of this transaction, Foster's will achieve a more diverse shareholder base," Kunkel said.
"This ends the uncertainty of the perceived market overhang of the major shareholdings."
